chapter_theme: Three songs at Sri Purushamangai (ஸ்ரீ புருஷமங்கை): pleas against women's eyes and the waste of wealth on them, and for the supreme of Vedanta beyond the senses and the mind's maya, with praise of Rama and Krishna as Murugan's uncle.

968.reading: The poet asks that he not, infatuated by the breasts of women whose eyes are Kama's arrows, fail to bow with justice and love to the feet of the First Guru and so waste in mind and body; that he stand apart from the work of the five senses, which stand like hunters, and the four inner instruments, and understand and receive grace; and that Murugan come and end his craving, defeat the maya of thought and grant the supreme reality at the end of the Veda. The praise tells Rama's story, Tataka's death, the guarding of Vishvamitra's sacrifice, the breaking of the bow, marriage to Janaki and giving up the crown for a mother's word, names Murugan his nephew, and pictures his peacock dancing so that Adisesha's heads shake, at Sri Purushamangai.
968.nuance: வேடர் என நின்ற ஐம்புலன் நாலு கரணங்கள்: the senses are hunters and the inner instruments (mind, intellect, ego, thought) are named as four; release is standing apart from their work (தொழில் வேறுபட நின்று). வேதமுடிவின் பரம்பொருள் is the supreme of Vedanta.

969.reading: The poet speaks of women with loosened hair and swinging earrings who stir desire, whose breasts stand firm against lovers, and whose eyes are a net in which his great understanding was lost; with a heart tossed in love, he asks Murugan to come, stand before him and give grace to end his trouble. The praise names Kanda on the one peacock with the vel and anklets, son of Uma, holder of the cock-banner, the life of Senthil, and the lord of Sri Purushamangai with its chariot streets, fragrant groves and high pools.
969.nuance: கண்கள் வலையாலே பேரறிவு குந்து: the eyes are a net that takes away understanding. மந்தி தந்தி வாரண அனங்கன் is a string of comparisons whose sense is unclear. The praise names Senthil though the song is placed at Purushamangai.

970.reading: The poet says that, pained by the five arrows of Kama in spring, he went to women standing in every street, came at the right hour, fell at their feet, talked much friendship, drank the nectar of their honeyed mouths and sank into their cool breasts, and worked until the wealth he had sought ran to waste; he asks whether he must wander without any goal. The praise names Murugan nephew of Krishna, who drove the cattle, measured the earth, slept on a banyan leaf and stirred the milk and curd in cowherd homes, the one whose chest shines with the deer-girl of the hunters, at Sri Purushamangai, where the Vedas sound.
970.nuance: தேடிய தனங்கள் பாழ்பட: money earned and wasted on the women of the street is what leaves him with no goal (சேர்கதி அதின்றி).

links.note: Both tie the courtesan's company to money: the Naladiyar's love lasts as long as a lamp's oil, and 970 ends with the wealth sought now wasted and no goal left.
